title: Shock tube, air at rest released across a pressure jump (Sod's problem)

outcome.label: Completed, with differences from what was expected
outcome.note: This report was written before the wording changed on 15 November 2026. Where its text says FAIL or FAILED, a result missed a limit that the agent set for itself before the runs. The experiment itself did not fail.

goal: The first flow with shock waves. Step 1 of 7 on the way to a rotating detonation engine.
story: Solved first with OpenFOAM's shock solver, which the project had never used. gpucfd had no solver for a gas whose density changes. One was built the same day and run on the same problem and grids, with its settings chosen by a budget of twelve short runs fixed in advance.

requirements: A closed tube of air at rest, 1 m long. A thin wall in the middle separates high pressure on the left from low pressure on the right.
The wall is removed. A shock wave runs to the right and an expansion to the left. No friction and no heat conduction.

Asked for at half a millisecond: density, velocity and pressure along the tube, the states between the waves, where each wave is, whether mass and energy are kept, and how sharp the computed jumps are.
Reference: the exact solution of this problem.
Pass limits: written by the solver agent before its fine runs.

results.headline: OpenFOAM's shock solver converges to the exact solution of the shock tube: on 12800 cells the mean errors are \(0.0085\,\%\) (density), \(0.012\,\%\) (velocity), \(0.0068\,\%\) (pressure), the states between the waves are within \(0.0022\,\%\) and mass and energy are kept to round-off. But the pressure error falls more slowly than the limit set before the runs assumed (order \(0.78\) against \(0.85\)): \(0.0068\,\%\) against a limit of \(0.0055\,\%\). gpucfd's new solver for gas with shocks runs the same grids with errors 2.1 to 3.2 times smaller than OpenFOAM's on the finest grid, in 11090 steps against 23040 and 1.2 s against 84 s.
meaning: OpenFOAM's shock solver gets the exact answer to about a hundredth of a per cent, puts every wave in the right place, and keeps mass and energy exactly.
One expectation was not met: the pressure error fell more slowly with the grid than the agent had predicted before its fine runs. The answer itself is accurate.
gpucfd's new solver is two to three times more accurate on the finest grid, in half the time steps.
For the detonation engine: a shock is spread over 2 cells on every grid, and this solver needs half the time step its own examples use, or the pressure rings behind the shock.
limits: The two tools were not given the same care: OpenFOAM ran as the solver agent set it up, on one core and not tuned for speed. gpucfd's method was chosen by twelve short tries.
Why OpenFOAM's error in the expansion falls slowly is not explained. gpucfd with the same kind of limiter does not show it, so it belongs to OpenFOAM's solver and not to the limiter.
One dimension and no friction. The time step is not converged: the full report says how much error is left.
answer: OpenFOAM matches the exact solution to about a hundredth of a per cent, with every wave in the right place.
gpucfd, built for this case and run on the same grids, is two to three times closer still, and much faster.
One prediction of the agent was missed: OpenFOAM's pressure error shrinks more slowly with finer grids than it expected. The answer itself is accurate.

accuracy.note: Each number is how far the computed value is from the exact solution, on the finest grid (12 800 cells). Zero would be a perfect match. A percentage is that distance as a share of the exact value. A distance in mm says how far a computed wave sits from where the exact solution puts it, in a tube 1 m long (minus: further left).

speed.note: Four of the eight grids. Cells and time step are halved together, so each level costs four times the one before. A gpucfd step has three stages, an OpenFOAM step one. In one dimension the GPU is mostly idle, so gpucfd's times measure its overhead, not the card. gpucfd's times run from creating the solver to the final field; starting the GPU library adds 0.22 s once.
